lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the future of war
lead.head: Swords, shields and software

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 112

body: When Amit Varma pro­posed an episode on the his­tory of war, Ajay Shah replied “fu­ture of war”, again and again, until Varma saw he had a dif­fer­ent idea. {#history}

Shah’s case was that much of what mil­i­taries know is al­ready out of date. Wars from 1967 to the Gulf War, he said, were still recog­nis­able by the stan­dards of the Second World War. The last five years are not.
“The world has changed below our feet,” he said.
Why study war at all? Early states, Shah said, re­ally did only one thing, wage war, and ab­hor­ring vi­o­lence does not make war go away.

Military his­tory moves in jumps. Aircraft car­ri­ers caught the Royal Navy off bal­ance, and German tanks with Stuka dive bombers stunned Poland and France. Behind such jumps, he said, lies an end­less dance be­tween the sword and the shield. {112-C02}
## Six hard sto­ries

Shah grounded his ar­gu­ment in six sto­ries. Ukraine, with no navy to speak of, drove Russia’s fleet from the Black Sea. Ukrainian drones, as­sem­bled in[[x1]] se­cret in­side Russia, flew out of trucks to strike five air bases. Mossad did much the same in­side Iran.
On the Ukrainian front, two ex­hausted armies face each other across a no man’s land up to 30 kilo­me­tres deep, where drones see any­thing that moves.
## Nine prin­ci­ples

From the sto­ries came nine prin­ci­ples. The first is that sur­prise and mass are gone: thanks to satel­lites, drones and open-source in­tel­li­gence, every im­por­tant cam­paign of the Russia-Ukraine war has been fully known to the other side. {112-C04}

Another is an in­ver­sion. At short range, de­fence now dom­i­nates. At long range, at­tack does: Ukrainian drones fly 1,000 to 2,000 kilo­me­tres into Russia and de­stroy fac­to­ries night after night.
“It is very easy to kill a fac­tory,” Shah said. “It is very dif­fi­cult to win a trench.” {112-C06}

Equipment, he ar­gued, has boiled down to some­thing that moves, some­thing that sees and some­thing that kills. “The rest is all soft­ware.” A new re­vi­sion pushed over the air be­comes an in­stant up­grade for the whole force. {112-C08}
## The up­shot

Conventional war, Shah said, is back de­spite nu­clear weapons. Soldiers must be prob­lem solvers, not merely brave. Factories must be able to surge in wartime, and pro­cure­ment should buy civil­ian tech­nol­ogy and move at the speed of Silicon Valley.
Above all, all roads lead to scale. Only the United States and China can reach it alone; ev­ery­one else, India in­cluded, must build with part­ners.

Varma, speak­ing as a layper­son, ended with two fears. Wars will move at be­wil­der­ing speed, tempt­ing both sides to hand de­ci­sions to AI. And a coun­try may not know whether it is at war at all, or with whom.
His hope was trade. “War helps no one, it’s a ter­ri­ble neg­a­tive sum game,” he said.
Shah agreed, while in­sist­ing that there is evil in the world and the state must be able to deal with it.
Varma’s farewell was four words: “Make trade, not war.”

second.label: The Ukraine front
second.head: One drone, one soldier
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a battlefield unlike any before it in world history

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the hellscape of the Ukraine front

body: Two ex­hausted armies face each other in Ukraine across a bat­tle­field like none other in world his­tory, Ajay Shah said. In the First World War, trenches sat one or two kilo­me­tres apart. Here, no man’s land is 10, 20, 30 kilo­me­tres deep. {#nomansland}

Drones from both sides watch it con­stantly[[x2]]. Mass five hun­dred men and fifty tanks for an at­tack and they will be seen, and pre­ci­sion-guided mu­ni­tions will de­stroy them. Russia, nearly out of Soviet equip­ment, has re­sorted to golf carts. {#golfcarts}

So sol­diers hud­dle and hide, man­ag­ing only small, dinky ac­tions day after day. “They will send one drone to kill one sol­dier,” Shah said. {112-S06} Amit Varma noted that tech­nol­ogy had ex­panded the hellscape, and it could grow fur­ther.

quote.text: This is the first time in world his­tory that you have cruel, un­re­lent­ing drone cov­er­age and pre­ci­sion guided mu­ni­tions.

third.head: Sand in the works

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the strange sand of the Sinai

body: In the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Ajay Shah said, Israeli equip­ment in the Sinai desert stopped work­ing prop­erly. Tank treads and tyres were af­fected, and he thought some bridg­ing equip­ment too, be­cause the sand had char­ac­ter­is­tics no­body had seen be­fore.
Then sci­en­tists “from the Weizmann Institute in Jerusalem came, sat there on the sand, did ex­per­i­ments with the sand, all while the war was going on”. {112-S11}
They went home and re­designed the bridg­ing gear, and that, Shah said, is how Israel won the Sinai. Amit Varma’s ver­dict: “Human soft­ware.”

Modern war, Shah ar­gued, is a game of more in­tel­li­gence[[x3]], so the mil­i­tary needs “wimps like Vaishnav”. Varma rose to his friend’s de­fence; Shah clar­i­fied that he meant “Vaishnav lev­els of ge­nius”. {112-J13}

box.title: The book that started it
box.text: Amit Varma had wanted a his­tory-of-war episode built on *Conflict* by David Petraeus and Andrew Roberts, a book on the re­cent evo­lu­tion of war­fare that he en­joyed a few months ago. Ajay Shah steered them to the fu­ture. {112-R01}

sections.label: Why war matters
sections.head: Peace was the easy part
sections.caption: why a pacifist must still study war
body: Why does a man who has railed against machismo care so much about war? Amit Varma put the ques­tion to Ajay Shah, who is in­vited to give talks to rooms full of gen­er­als.

Early states, Shah an­swered, re­ally did only one thing: they waged war. Creating peace at home was not that hard or that ex­pen­sive; by about 1900 the UK had fig­ured out crim­i­nal jus­tice. The fron­tier was war.

War forced states to build fis­cal sys­tems[[x8]] to raise money and to learn pub­lic pro­cure­ment. It has driven sci­en­tific in­no­va­tion again and again, and it shaped the very bound­aries of states.
So dis­lik­ing vi­o­lence is not enough. “A sim­ple in­sis­tence on paci­fism does not solve the prob­lem of war,” he said. {112-C01}
## Jumps, not steps

Force de­sign has been thrown off bal­ance again and again by new tech­nol­ogy, Shah said. Attack and de­fence take turns: “Sometimes de­vel­op­ment in the tech­niques of war favour the sword. So at­tack­ers get an upper hand. Sometimes they favour the shield.” {112-C02}
People joke, he said, that Israel’s army in 1967 was Second World War ca­pa­bil­ity fully re­alised. The Gulf War was “the first tri­umph of sil­i­con over steel”. Both were recog­nis­able. {112-J20}
Shah set the episode’s lim­its: no nu­clear war, no in­sur­gen­cies, just “sim­ple main­line con­ven­tional war with a peer op­po­nent”.
~ The les­son, he said, is never to fight the last war but al­ways to look for­ward.

quote.text: A sim­ple ab­hor­rence of cru­elty and vi­o­lence doesn’t put an end to war.

sections.label: Probability one
sections.head: A sky full of drones
sections.caption: drone swarms, lasers and 3D printers
body: Ajay Shah named three tech­nolo­gies that are not yet used at scale but, he said, are com­ing “with prob­a­bil­ity one”.
The first is drone swarms: ten drones on one mis­sion, talk­ing to each other, then a hun­dred, a thou­sand, 10,000, swarms he ex­pects to be “mad­den­ingly large”. {#swarm}
Amit Varma greeted the es­ca­la­tion with a sport­ing metaphor. {112-J09}
Shah asked lis­ten­ers to pic­ture 6 June 1944, when peo­ple in Normandy were woken around 3 am by Allied planes fly­ing from Britain for hours. That is the scene ahead, he said, ex­cept with drones.
## Light against the swarm
The sec­ond is Iron Beam, an Israeli sys­tem that fires lasers at drones. Imagine ten beams each killing ten drones a minute, Shah said, and 10,000 drones are not so scary. {#ironbeam}
The third is less glam­orous: 3D print­ers car­ried close to the front to print spare parts for equip­ment that is for­ever break­ing down.

Their friend Ayush Patnaik, Shah said, has built a 3D printer that prints ev­ery­thing about it­self ex­cept one noz­zle. Buy the noz­zle, give Ayush a milk­shake, and he will print you one. {112-J10}
~ Varma imag­ined aliens land­ing on Earth to find 3D print­ers the dom­i­nant species, with hu­mans re­duced to fos­sils.

quote.text: You just change the kitty party into a cricket match.

sections.label: The principles
sections.head: No surprises, no safe rear
sections.caption: nine principles for the new battlefield
body: Asked how he would re­vamp the mil­i­tary for the country’s grand leader, “a fel­low Gujarati”, Ajay Shah began with prin­ci­ples, not ac­tions. Great coun­tries, he said, are not built out of get­ting shit done. {112-C03}
Logistics has be­come far harder. The enemy can see your am­mu­ni­tion dumps and sup­ply trucks, and “a lo­gis­tics truck is even more im­por­tant than a tank”. {#truck}

Strategic wars are wars of economies[[x10]], and the in­tel­li­gence rev­o­lu­tion has made them hun­grier. Israel’s mil­i­tary fuses all its sen­sors into one tar­get­ing sys­tem, so tar­gets per day, and the burn rate of mu­ni­tions, have soared.
## The sol­dier as sen­sor
Some days, Shah said, a mod­ern sol­dier is not so much fight­ing as form fill­ing, re­port­ing his po­si­tion, his shells and the tank he thinks he sees. {112-C07}
That data lets an “Uber for ar­tillery”[[x9]] match a tar­get to the best-placed gun. Too much of it brings death by data, which he called the al­go­rith­mic fog of war.

His ninth and last prin­ci­ple was the pace of change. From September 1939 to Hiroshima, dogma was over­turned every few months, and he be­lieves this is such a mo­ment again: “stay­ing in the old ways is a cer­tainty of doing badly”. {112-C10}
~ Amit Varma called it a mas­ter­class and urged lis­ten­ers to de­cide which prin­ci­ples they dis­agree with.

quote.text: As much as send­ing bul­lets out, the sol­dier is bring­ing in­for­ma­tion back. And in­for­ma­tion is power.

sections.label: What India should do
sections.head: Small, cheap and many
sections.caption: what India should build, and how
body: Nuclear weapons, Ajay Shah said, have not made con­ven­tional war ob­so­lete. “No, con­ven­tional war is back.” {112-C12}
Amit Varma added that two guests on *The Seen and the Unseen* had made the coun­ter­in­tu­itive case that nu­clear weapons make con­ven­tional war more im­por­tant, not less.

War now burns mu­ni­tions faster than any peace­time fac­tory sup­plies, so Shah wants surge ca­pac­ity de­signed in: con­tracts for 100 tubes with the right, but not the obli­ga­tion, to take 300. {#tubes}
## Off the shelf

Buy civil­ian tech­nol­ogy wher­ever pos­si­ble, he said. Starlink, a high-volume prod­uct, has im­mense mil­i­tary value. If shore-based mis­siles on Great Nicobar could dom­i­nate the Straits of Malacca, do you need air­craft car­ri­ers there?
Procurement, he said, must swap ven­dors[[x11]] like Raytheon and McDonnell Douglas and 30-year cy­cles for some­thing closer to Silicon Valley. {112-C13}
Every sen­si­ble coun­try, he said, should send teams to Ukraine, today’s equiv­a­lent of the Spanish Civil War, where Hitler per­fected the Blitzkrieg. {112-C11}
Defence eco­nom­ics, Shah said, comes down to scale: only the United States and China can reach it alone, so ev­ery­one else must share gear with five to ten other coun­tries. {112-C14}
~ India, Shah sug­gested, could make weapons for a Poland-Ukraine-South Korea part­ner­ship, since a fac­tory in Tamil Nadu is far from any front.

quote.text: So we need to build surge ca­pa­bil­i­ties into or­di­nary peace­time de­fence pro­cure­ment, rather than run­ning around when a war comes.

sections.label: Two fears, one hope
sections.head: The last human decision
sections.caption: two fears and one exhortation
body: Amit Varma came with two fears and one hope. The first fear began with Vasili Arkhipov, the Soviet sub­ma­rine of­fi­cer who re­fused to fire a nu­clear tor­pedo in 1962.[[x13]]
Future wars, Varma said, will move at be­wil­der­ing speed, and every side will be tempted to hand de­ci­sions to AI. Mistakes at that scale could be cat­a­strophic. {112-C16}

His sec­ond fear was a new fog of war. A power cut, a GST or Aadhaar back­end fail­ure, con­tam­i­nated water: is it an ac­ci­dent, ter­ror­ism or war?[[x12]] And is the cul­prit Pakistan, China, a dis­si­dent group, or the state in a false flag? {112-C17}
## Citizens, not sub­jects

Against them he set one hope: trade. Humanity has flour­ished through trade and peace­ful co­op­er­a­tion, never war, he said; India should trade with China and Pakistan, and mu­si­cians on both sides should keep jam­ming. {112-C18}
His ex­hor­ta­tion was to act as cit­i­zens: de­mand a state ready for fu­ture war, but one that ac­tively makes peace with its neigh­bours.

Ajay Shah agreed, adding that there is evil in the world. He sug­gested doing for con­ven­tional war what Johnny von Neumann, John Nash and Thomas Schelling did for nu­clear weapons after 1945: doc­trines that pro­duce more peace.
~ Varma hoped none of their worst fears come true, and that we trade until we can trade no more. {112-J16}

quote.text: What if the last human de­ci­sion in a war is a de­ci­sion to start the war?

But if you ac­tu­ally look at the wider flour­ish­ing of hu­man­ity, the wider flour­ish­ing of hu­man­ity has never hap­pened through war, it has al­ways hap­pened through trade, through peace­ful co­op­er­a­tion

p3.title: War stories
p3.deck: Drones from trucks, boats that fire back, and one officer’s calm veto

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Ukrainian raid that began inside Russia
stories.head: Russia caught in a Spider Web
body: Over 18 months, Ajay Shah said, Ukrainian spe­cial forces shipped equip­ment and ma­te­ri­als into safe houses in­side Russia. One, they en­joyed point­ing out, was in a build­ing right next to an FSB of­fice.
There they set up 3D print­ers, gath­ered parts and ex­plo­sives and as­sem­bled 117 at­tack drones. Nothing was shipped in ready-made. {#attack-drones}

The drones were hid­den in ship­ping con­tain­ers on trucks. Each driver was an or­di­nary com­mer­cial driver, told some story and sent to wait at a pin on Google Maps, five to ten kilo­me­tres from one of five air bases: out­side the fence, on civil­ian roads where no­body fusses over a parked truck.
By the time the trucks moved, not a sin­gle Ukrainian was left in Russia. Someone in Ukraine pressed a but­ton, the roofs of the con­tain­ers opened, and the drones flew out.

They rode or­di­nary data SIMs on the Russian mo­bile net­work, and some video is be­lieved to have streamed over Telegram. They may even have car­ried on­board AI and a table of Russia’s costli­est planes.

About twenty planes, cen­tral to the nightly bomb­ing of Ukraine and worth per­haps two or three bil­lion dol­lars, are be­lieved to have been de­stroyed by drones cost­ing about half a mil­lion dol­lars. {#halfmillion}
Zelensky an­nounced that the op­er­a­tion had been 18 months in the mak­ing. “And that just makes you think what else are they work­ing on?” Shah said. {112-S07}
~ Amit Varma added his favourite de­tail: the con­tain­ers had false ceil­ings, so a cop who opened one would find noth­ing.
stories.why: Commercial off-the-shelf parts, a mo­bile data SIM and pa­tience let a weaker coun­try hit planes deep in­side a stronger one. For Shah, a country’s in­te­rior is no longer safe, and every mil­i­tary plan­ner should be think­ing about such threats.
stories.postscript: Shah’s test for lis­ten­ers: a gen­uine mil­i­tary geek knows the names of all the op­er­a­tions. This one, he said, will go down in his­tory. {112-J06}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Operation Spider Web

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a country with no navy won at sea
stories.head: Who needs a navy?
body: Early in the war, Ajay Shah be­lieves, Ukraine’s navy was a sin­gle ship, which it scut­tled so that the Russians could not cap­ture it. {#nonavy}

Russia’s fleet sat in Sevastopol. Ukraine an­swered with three in­no­va­tions. Drones and NATO-quality in­tel­li­gence tracked every Russian ship in real time; shore-based mis­siles skim­ming two me­tres above the waves sank the Moskva; and drone boats car­ried a thou­sand kg of ex­plo­sive. When Russian he­li­copters hunted the boats, they were re­designed to fire anti-air mis­siles back.

Russia stopped using Sevastopol, and Ukrainian com­mer­cial ships ply the Black Sea again. Shah cred­ited a cul­ture of en­gi­neer­ing under fire: “I want to get an in­no­va­tion out in the field next week.” {112-S05}
~ Shah rel­ished the image of an ar­ro­gant he­li­copter, “the god of the sky”, shot down by a dumb boat. {112-J04}
stories.why: Amit Varma saw in­cen­tives at work: at a break­fast of bacon and eggs, the chicken is in­ter­ested but the pig is com­mit­ted, “and in that sense, Ukraine is a pig.” As his rid­dle went, the hare runs for his life. {112-J03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the battle for the Black Sea

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Israel’s drones from inside Iran
stories.head: The lion that rose from within
body: Mossad op­er­a­tives, Ajay Shah said, built a safe house in­side Iran, shipped parts to them­selves and used 3D print­ers to build large num­bers of drones. Nobody yet knows how many.
In a syn­chro­nised as­sault, the drones took off in­side Iran and knocked out a great deal of its air de­fences. Then Israeli planes ar­rived and hit tar­gets all over the coun­try.

Whether the nu­clear pro­gramme was stopped is un­known; per­haps 400 kilo­grams of 60 per cent en­riched ura­nium is still sit­ting around in Iran. {#uranium} But Iran’s con­ven­tional power, Shah said, was set back five or ten years. Iran hit back with prob­a­bly 1,000 mis­siles and drones; about fifty, it is es­ti­mated, got through. {#fifty}
~ Shah called it a fas­ci­nat­ing story of com­bin­ing long-range ac­tion from Israel with covert op­er­a­tions in­side Iran.

quote.text: So Israeli air de­fence is so great that es­sen­tially ev­ery­thing got killed in the sky.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma had a quiz: if the 1970s actor Ajit took part in an up­ris­ing, what would it be called? Operation Rising Loin. {112-J08}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Operation Rising Lion

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Soviet officer’s veto in 1962
stories.head: The man who said ‘hold on’
body: In October 1962, Amit Varma said, dur­ing the Cuban Missile Crisis, a Soviet sub­ma­rine called the B-59 was in the wa­ters off Cuba, car­ry­ing nu­clear tor­pe­does. At one point it came under at­tack.
Its cap­tain thought the two coun­tries were at war and that it was time to fire. But a launch needed three sign-offs: the cap­tain, the po­lit­i­cal of­fi­cer and the first of­fi­cer.
The first of­fi­cer, ef­fec­tively sec­ond in com­mand, was Vasili Arkhipov. Hold on, he said: if we are wrong, a nu­clear first strike could set off a world war. He ex­er­cised his veto. {112-S12}
~ The tor­pedo was not fired, Varma said, “be­cause one man was able to sit down and take a calm de­ci­sion”.
stories.why: Process, and one calm per­son, kept a nu­clear tor­pedo un­fired. Varma told the story to frame his first fear: that wars fought at ma­chine speed will tempt both sides to leave no room for such a pause. {112-C16}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Vasili Arkhipov’s veto

quiz.q: Where did Indian and Pakistani planes stay while firing at each other, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: High over their own ter­ri­tory, fir­ing stand­off weapons be­yond vis­ual range.

quiz.q: How quickly did Ukraine want new ideas on the battlefield, in Ajay Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: Next week: not lessons for a fu­ture war, but in­no­va­tions in this one.

quiz.q: Who came to the Sinai battlefield in 1973 to experiment with its strange sand?
quiz.a: Scientists from the Weizmann Institute, who went home and re­designed the bridg­ing gear.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s IIT wingmate Ajay Bhagavat say makes manufacturing harder than services?
quiz.a: Operating mar­gins rarely top 15 per cent, leav­ing lit­tle cash to pay for learn­ing.

quiz.q: Where, according to Ajay Shah, did Adolf Hitler perfect the Blitzkrieg?
quiz.a: In the Spanish Civil War of 1936, the lab of its day.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s riddle, who runs faster, the fox or the hare, and why?
quiz.a: The hare: the fox runs only for his lunch, the hare for his life.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 112. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Vasili Arkhipov (Image courtesy by Olga Arkhipova, CC BY-SA 4.0); David Petraeus (Darren Livingston, public domain); John von Neumann (Wikimedia Commons, Attribution); Andrew Roberts (©House of Lords / photography by Roger Harris, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Conflict
shelf.creator: David Petraeus & Andrew Roberts
shelf.why: A book on the re­cent his­tory and evo­lu­tion of war­fare that Amit en­joyed a few months ago and found full of things he didn’t know.

shelf.title: Gokhale: The Indian Moderates and the British Raj
shelf.creator: B.R. Nanda
shelf.why: A win­dow into Gokhale and the rad­i­cal in­tel­lec­tual cul­ture of late-nineteenth-century Pune.

shelf.title: The World in 2050 (Ep 106 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A play­ful but se­ri­ous at­tempt to imag­ine the world 25 years out, from swarms of cheap drones in war to how re­la­tion­ships might be or­gan­ised once love, sex, com­pan­ion­ship and par­ent­ing come apart.

shelf.title: The Age of Hybrid Warfare (Ep 84 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why, in mod­ern con­flict, you may not know whether you have been at­tacked or by whom, and why covert, op­por­tunis­tic at­tacks such as crip­pling an­other country’s pay­roll sys­tem are the strat­egy of rogue na­tions and back­fire in the long run.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military (Ep 31 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay, who speaks to rooms full of gen­er­als, on re­form­ing India’s mil­i­tary, start­ing with pen­sions: with­out fix­ing them there is no money for a mod­ern mil­i­tary.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Ep 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Ep 14 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

shelf.title: The WRONG Way to Fight Extremists (Ep 4 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is where they cover in­sur­gen­cies and coun­terin­sur­gency, which this episode de­lib­er­ately skips.

shelf.title: What Just Happened Between India & Pakistan? (Ep 418 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane & Aditya Ramanathan
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion recorded as events un­folded, with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan, on the lat­est India-Pakistan clash, which showed both sides using fairly ad­vanced equip­ment.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Ep 32 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

shelf.title: Is the Singularity Near? (Ep 2 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ early episode on AI, with Amit’s ar­gu­ment that AGI is about five years away and eas­ier to reach than peo­ple as­sume.

shelf.title: India in the Nuclear Age (Ep 80 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Prakash Menon
shelf.why: It ex­plores the coun­ter­in­tu­itive idea that nu­clear weapons make con­ven­tional war more im­por­tant, not less.

shelf.title: The India-Pakistan Conflict (Ep 111 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
shelf.why: Srinath Raghavan on India-Pakistan re­la­tions and, in great de­tail, the his­tory of the Kashmir prob­lem; Amit cites it for the view that the nu­clear shadow doesn’t make con­ven­tional war go away.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (Ep 95 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: More Ammo: Improving Resilience Against Extreme Surges in Demand
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It pro­poses op­tion-style de­fence con­tracts, for ex­am­ple 100 units a month with the right but not the obli­ga­tion to go to 300.

shelf.title: The Power of Moore’s Laws (Ep 87 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Built around Wright’s Law: pro­duc­tiv­ity rises about 20% with each dou­bling of cu­mu­la­tive out­put, so vol­ume drives down costs and tiny fac­to­ries can’t com­pete, in ser­vices as well as man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Ep 104 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of why Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is weak: eight ways it dif­fers from ser­vices, twelve things that hob­ble it in India (from du­ties on im­ported in­puts to labour laws) and seven items for every state’s growth strat­egy.

shelf.title: Is Manufacturing the Answer? (Ep 105 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The se­quel to What Ails Indian Manufacturing?, which dis­man­tles the myth of man­u­fac­tur­ing as un­skilled as­sem­bly-line labour.

laughs.text: Amit says Ajay’s pitch for a fu­ture-of-war episode felt like ‘a glitch in the ma­trix, in other words, Deja Vu’, since they’d al­ready cov­ered hy­brid war­fare and the world in 2050. He adds: ‘We are not like other YouTube chan­nels that we will re­cy­cle our old ma­te­rial and re­peat our­selves as you know, men with egos tend to do. Shameful. Absolutely shame­ful.’

Amit on why Ukraine in­no­vates so fu­ri­ously: ‘when you have a break­fast of bacon and eggs, what is the dif­fer­ence be­tween the chicken and the pig? And the an­swer is that the chicken is in­ter­ested, but the pig is com­mit­ted. And in that sense, Ukraine is a pig.’

Ajay on a Russian he­li­copter hunt­ing a Ukrainian drone boat: ‘Just think of the ar­ro­gance and the con­fi­dence of a he­li­copter. You feel you are the god of the sky, and you’re look­ing down at a dumb boat... and the boat says, Oops, and it just puts up its hand and a mis­sile flies out of the boat and shoots down a he­li­copter.’
On the false ceil­ings that hid the Spider Web drones, Ajay notes you only need about six inches. Amit: ‘You just need six inches, that’s what she said.’

Amit, hav­ing es­tab­lished that Ajay is no ex­pert on Indian mass cul­ture, asks a quiz any­way: ‘if the fa­mous nine­teen sev­en­ties actor Ajit was to take part in an up­ris­ing, what would that up­ris­ing be called? Operation Rising Loin.’

Ajay’s friend Ayush Patnaik built a 3D printer that prints ev­ery­thing about it­self ex­cept one noz­zle: ‘you have to buy one noz­zle and then you have to give Ayush one milk shake and he will print a three D printer for you.’ Amit ex­trap­o­lates that with some AGI, aliens land­ing on Earth ‘will think that the dom­i­nant species here are these three D print­ers. And us hu­mans there’ll be some fos­sils around.’ Ajay tops it: ‘There is an­other amaz­ing path­way to a 3D printer which is called a woman.’

Ajay on his or­gan­i­sa­tion: ‘in my or­ga­ni­za­tion, XKDR Forum, we are crazy geeks. We in ad­di­tion to lov­ing FDI and lov­ing our pro­gram­ming, we also love gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing. We think gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing is hot.’

Ajay’s test for lis­ten­ers: ‘put on your sort­ing hat and clas­sify your­self that are you a gen­uine mil­i­tary geek or are you fake? A gen­uine mil­i­tary geek knows the names of all the op­er­a­tions.’ He lists Barbarossa, Citadel and Market Garden, and says Operation Spider Web will join them in his­tory.

D-Day, 6 June 1944: Normandy res­i­dents were woken around 3 am by the drone of thou­sands of Allied planes fly­ing for hours from Britain. Ajay says this is what thou­sand-strong drone swarms will look like.
The Spanish Civil War of 1936 as the lab ‘where Adolf Hitler per­fected the Blitzkrieg’. It is Ajay’s anal­ogy for why every mil­i­tary should study Ukraine up close.

Israel’s 1967 war, which peo­ple joke was Second World War ca­pa­bil­ity fully re­alised, and the Gulf War as ‘the first tri­umph of sil­i­con over steel’. Ajay uses them as the last ‘recognisable’ wars be­fore today’s break.
